## Conceptual Alignment Between Dynamical Resilience and Homeostatic Plasticity

Homeostatic plasticity (HP) is one of the mechanisms of metaplasticity, referring to the capacity of neurons and neural circuits to regulate their own excitability and synaptic strength relative to the overall activity of the network to maintain stability, thereby influencing the future potential for Hebbian forms of plasticity (10.1016/j.conb.2018.08.010). This conceptualization of HP resonates with the definition of resilience proposed by Scheffer et al. (10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2024.0215) within the dynamical systems framework. Dynamical resilience is defined as the capacity of a system to absorb perturbations without transitioning into alternative pathological attractors. In Scheffer's model, the healthy mental state possesses a basin of attraction whose depth reflects resilience. In a resilient basin, the system can easily return to equilibrium despite transient disturbances. As this basin loses resilience, the risk increases that minor stressors can precipitate a transition into disordered states.

Homeostatic plasticity encompasses a suite of compensatory mechanisms, including synaptic scaling, intrinsic excitability adjustments, and metaplastic modulation of synaptic weights (10.1111/j.1460-9568.2006.05203.x;10.1038/nrn1327;10.1016/j.cell.2008.10.008; 10.1016/j.neuropharm.2013.07.009). These implement feedback control loops that counteract deviations from set-point activity levels. When a neural circuit experiences sustained increases in excitatory drive, homeostatic downscaling of excitatory synapses and/or upregulation of inhibitory transmission restores balance. Conversely, prolonged suppression of activity triggers compensatory strengthening of excitatory connections or reduction of inhibitory drive (10.1038/36103).

The metaphorical equivalence becomes apparent when considering that HP provides the feedback mechanisms necessary to maintain the basin of attraction. Just as dynamical resilience reflects the capacity to return to baseline, HP represents the neurobiological machinery that ensures a return to the functional set-point. Extending the concept to the psychological domain, high resilience implies the ability to withstand stressors and rapidly return to mental equilibrium.

## Empirical Evidence for Homeostatic Plasticity and Stress Resilience

Empirical evidence suggests that HP at the circuit level mediates stress resilience at the behavioral level. Research on mesolimbic dopamine circuits has shown that homeostatic adaptations following chronic social defeat stress distinguish resilient from susceptible animals (10.1016/j.cell.2007.09.018;10.1038/nn.4245). Specifically, animals exhibiting behavioral resilience demonstrate compensatory synaptic adjustments in ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons that normalize circuit excitability despite ongoing stress exposure (10.1126/science.1249240). BDNF is also implicated in HP mechanisms. Animals with enhanced BDNF signaling exhibit greater capacity for homeostatic synaptic adjustments and correspondingly greater behavioral resilience to chronic stress (10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5725-10.2011;10.1016/j.pneurobio.2022.102333).

The concept of "homeostatic disruption or failure" is relevant in understanding depression (10.1016/s0306-9877(96)90152-8; 10.1186/s13578-025-01369-y;10.1016/j.jagp.2019.07.016 ). Prolonged or severe perturbations can exhaust homeostatic mechanisms, leading to paradoxical or maladaptive compensatory responses (10.1016/j.biopsych.2024.09.026;10.1016/j.biopsych.2024.09.026). For instance, chronic stress can lead to excessive upregulation of inhibitory transmission in reward circuits, potentially contributing to anhedonia and motivational deficits. What began as a homeostatic response becomes pathological, contributing to the formation of a stable depressive attractor. This aligns with the dynamical systems concept of increasing "bad resilience"—the pathological state becomes increasingly resistant to interventions as maladaptive homeostatic adjustments entrench the disordered circuit configuration (10.1515/RNS.2011.044;10.1038/s41380-020-0686-8; 10.1016/j.ynstr.2017.05.001;).

## Clinical implication of Homeostatic Plasticity

Even if the brain's attractor landscape is restored to a healthy state according to the DMR model, maintaining this fragile recovery and preventing relapse necessitates robust HP regulation. HP has essential role in maintaining network stability (10.1111/jnc.13687;10.1073/pnas.1918368117). If HP remains compromised, minor perturbations—such as acute stressors, sleep deprivation, or circadian misalignment—can readily precipitate a transition back into a pathological state. Consequently, the final stage of the DMR sequence must involve the reinforcement of HP to stabilize the healthy attractor and enhance long-term resilience (10.1038/mp.2017.225).

rTMS, particularly theta burst stimulation (TBS) protocols, has been shown to induce metaplastic effects consistent with homeostatic regulation (10.1152/jn.00630.2015; 10.1038/s41598-018-26791-w). Depending on whether the protocol is continuous or intermittent, TBS can induce either LTD or LTP. Furthermore, the magnitude of these effects is modulated by the prior history of circuit activity (10.1007/s00429-023-02634-x). In individuals with depression, prefrontal circuits often exhibit abnormal metaplasticity characterized by blunted responses to plasticity-inducing protocols (10.1177/1759091417711512). If repeated stimulation sessions were to normalize this metaplastic deficit, it would significantly reduce the risk of relapse by enhancing resilience against future perturbations (10.1016/j.neuron.2020.05.015).

Several pharmacological agents show evidence of promoting homeostatic plasticity, suggesting potential for relapse prevention. Lithium has been shown to promote homeostatic downscaling of excitatory synaptic strength through effects on glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) signaling. This homeostatic adjustment may stabilize circuits prone to excessive excitability, thereby deepening the basin of attraction around euthymic states ( 10.1034/j.1399-5618.1999.010205.x;10.1016/j.neuron.2020.05.015;10.1016/j.jad.2017.12.026;10.7554/eLife.25480).

Valproate, for example, modulates GABAergic inhibition and has been shown to affect activity-dependent homeostatic plasticity in preclinical models (10.1016/j.pnpbp.2012.01.017;10.1016/s0278-6915(03)00195-9). Its efficacy in preventing both manic and depressive episodes may reflect stabilization of circuits prone to excessive excitability or hypoactivity through enhanced homeostatic regulation.

Novel compounds targeting metaplastic mechanisms may offer more direct approaches to enhancing homeostatic plasticity. For example, drugs modulating metabotropic glutamate receptors (particularly mGluR2/3 and mGluR5) can shift the threshold for synaptic plasticity induction and affect homeostatic scaling mechanisms (10.1016/j.neuron.2010.11.008;10.1016/j.neuron.2010.01.016 ). Similarly, agents affecting neurosteroid synthesis—which modulate GABAA receptor function and have rapid antidepressant effects—may act partly by restoring E-I balance through homeostatic mechanisms (10.1111/jne.12996;10.1038/s41398-023-02514-2).
